item.title: This is what's occurred to carried interest payments at Blackstone this year
item.description:
Blackstone reported its second quarter results today. They are pretty good. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-23/blackstone-profits-jump-boosted-by-exits-and-winning-bets-on-ai?srnd=all> notes that distributable earnings are up 26%. CEO Steven Schwarzman declared <https://s23.q4cdn.com/714267708/files/doc_financials/2026/q2/Blackstone2Q26EarningsPressRelease.pdf>it an "outstanding" second quarter and said it helped that Blackstone had decided to "lean in" to AI, thus becoming a "trusted partner at scale" to the 'innovators in the ecosystem.'
This sounds great. And for the moment at least, it also looks like some great things are happening to Blackstone's pay.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The chart below shows realized year to date performance compensation for Blackstone's key segments in the first half of 2026 versus last year. Realized performance compensation mostly represents the carried interest </news/what-is-carried-interest> that's actually been paid to employees from businesses Blackstone has successfully exited.
As the chart above shows, it's also been an outstanding start to the year for carried interest across most of Blackstone's investing segments. Best of all for carried interest was multi-asset investing, which comprises Blackstone's discretionary hedge fund allocation business, plus its multistrategy direct investment platform, which is Blackstone's own multistrategy hedge fund. Real estate professionals also experienced a more than tripling of their carried interest payments.
Blackstone's private equity professionals had to tolerate a mere 50% rise. Within private equity, it seems that infrastructure investors might best placed based on the chart below (which shows realized and unrealized gains in Q2 and the trailing previous 12 months.)
Source: Blackstone
The only segment where carried interest payments at Blackstone didn't increase year-on-year in the first half was credit and insurance, where they fell 51%. This might be because private credit investments at the firm generated a not-so-outstanding return of 0.4% net during the second quarter.
Blackstone's carried interest payments may decline in the second half of the year. In a footnote to today's results, Blackstone says employees can get carried interest payments that are higher than expected in some quarters and offset by lower fee related payments later in the year.

item.title: Deutsche Bank rehired a banker as a vice chairman. He left two years later for Santander
item.description:
Generally, when you bring back a former employee and sing their praises in an internal memo, you expect them to stick around for more than a few years. Deutsche Bank </news/deutsche-bank-q1-results>may, therefore, be sad to see the back of Simon Leopold, whom it rehired just two years ago, as he leaves for Santander.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Leopold joined the Spanish bank in New York last week according to FINRA's BrokerCheck tool. His LinkedIn states that his new role is head of US real estate investment banking, succeeding Steffen Doyle who departed the bank in December. Doyle was one of many Credit Suisse MDs that Santander hired after the Swiss bank collapsed; although Santander's corporate and investment bank became much more profitable <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-03-05/santander-s-us-investment-bank-profit-surges-after-hiring-spree> after their arrival, insiders told us around the time that these new colleagues weren't universally popular. </news/santander-insiders-say-credit-suisse-colleagues-spoiled-their-culture>
At Deutsche Bank, Leopold spent the last two years as vice chairman of the bank's real estate, gaming, lodging and leisure group. He spent 12 more years at the bank in his first stint, leaving as an MD in 2011. Since leaving, he became an MD at UBS and chief financial officer at a four different firms. Prior to rejoining Deutsche Bank, he was CFO of retail real estate firm Washington Prime Group.
In a 2024 memo seen by Bloomberg, <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-06-04/deutsche-bank-rehires-simon-leopold-as-a-vice-chairman>Reza Akhavi and Andrew Bartrop, co-heads of Deutsche Bank's real estate group, said Leopold "has developed deep, high-quality relationships" across the real estate space since he first left. Those relationships may soon follow him to Santander.

item.title: Goldman Sachs hired a JPMorgan equities ED in Hong Kong & may be paying her handsomely
item.description:
This is a good year to work in Asian equities. It's such a good year that the FT <https://www.ft.com/content/2dc8d54c-89b7-4e57-bd43-084d9edf01a4?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reported this week that banks are redirecting capital towards Asia and are foregoing opportunities elsewhere. As Asian equities trading volumes rise, so does demand for derivatives to hedge Asian markets. And so does demand for people who can sell them.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Against this backdrop, we understand that Goldman Sachs has poached Elena Su from JPMorgan in Hong Kong. Both Goldman and JPMorgan declined to comment on Su's change of seat. Su, whom we estimate to be in her late 20s, didn't respond to an invitation to confirm it. There are vague suggestions that she may have moved for $500k.
Su is the latest addition to Goldman's Hong Kong equities bench. The US bank hired John Lee from UBS in June. It also hired Leo Kim from SocGen and Jacky Pun from Mizuho, among others.
Insiders suggest Su is a reasonably big deal. She spent nearly seven years at JPMorgan in New York and then Hong Kong and graduated in financial economics from Columbia University. She was a flow and exotic derivatives salesperson for the bank.
Su was not educated in France. As we reported </news/french-equity-derivative-traders-are-more-popular-then-ever-not-just-with-banks> earlier this week, French exotic equities traders have also been the beneficiaries of rising demand in their space.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Curious case of the finance CEO not in a romantic relationship with a subordinate. M&A bankers are not on fire at BNP Paribas
item.description:
When John Neal, ex-chief executive of insurance broker Lloyd's of London stepped down as CEO after six years in January 2025, Lloyds seemed a bit regretful. Neal had delivered some "outstanding financial performance," it said. <https://www.lloyds.com/insights/media-centre/press-releases/lloyds-ceo-to-leave>He'd also been "instrumental" in promoting the insurance industry to "critical stakeholders." Neal sounded like a fun guy. For his part, Neal said he was "forever grateful" to his colleagues there. A LinkedIn post <https://www.linkedin.com/posts/johnneallloydsceo_farewell-to-lloyds-as-i-step-down-activity-7334187772070555648-i8l4?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAAAC_n9ABKGyf486Jq5_52e4WCygx5h9EouQ> showed him giving a valedictory speech in a flower-filled atrium while those colleagues looked on in mournful deference.
Since then, the flowers have wilted. Yesterday, Lloyd's issued a statement <https://www.lloyds.com/insights/media-centre/news/lloyds-finds-former-ceo-breached-compliance-rules>saying that if Neal still had deferred stock bonuses, it would withhold them. His reign was marked by "serious failings," "serious failures" and conduct "detrimental to the interests" of Lloyd's, said Lloyd's. If Neal is still grateful, his ex-colleagues are not.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
What occurred to change Lloyd's mind? Unproven allegations of a romantic relationship with a subordinate. Neal was accused of giving preferential treatment to his chief corporate affairs officer, a woman whom we estimate to be around 20 years his junior. There were suggestions of an unfair promotion. Senior people at Lloyd's raised concerns. Lloyd's says Neal undertook to modify his conduct, but did not do so in a "material" way.
The claims have taken their toll on Neal's career. He left Lloyd's to join Aon; then he dropped Aon to join AIG; <https://www.insurancetimes.co.uk/news/ex-lloyds-boss-neal-reverses-aon-move-to-join-aig/1455811.article> then AIG said he wouldn't join due to "personal circumstances." However, things are looking up. In a message to us yesterday, Neal said he now feels vindicated and able to move on. "I look back on my time at Lloyd's with real pride, and wish the Corporation and the Market every continued success in and for the future. My focus is solely on what’s next in my career.”
Neal's vindication comes from the fact that even after a lengthy investigation by a law firm, Lloyd's said it was unable to find "conclusive evidence" that he was in a relationship with the chief corporate affairs officer. Nor was it able to find process failures relating to her promotion. The chief corporate affairs officer has engaged her own lawyer who told the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/9cafc59d-d1f8-42d9-8100-c6dcb61250ee?syn-25a6b1a6=1> that Lloyd's had decided against her client "on the pretext of ‘perception’, the source of which was rumour, gossip and innuendo.” Neal himself tells us he was not at all surprised that the investigation found no inappropriate relationship and that this was "never in doubt."
Why would Lloyd's like to retain Neal's stock, then? It points to his incorrect handling of whistleblowing reports, his failure to modify undefined elements of his conduct in relation to the corporate affairs officer with whom he was at least found to be "sufficiently close" that eyebrows might be raised, and failure to meet "the standards of judgement, transparency and accountability expected of a Lloyd's Chief Executive." Neal also declined to handover his phone for his text messages to be scrutinised.
It's notable that Lloyd's can't retain Neal's deferred stock anyway. He gave it back when he left for AIG. But if it could, this is why Lloyd's says it would.
Despite the vindication, none of this sounds like a great reference. In the midst of intern season in investment banks, it should be a reminder that irreproachable behaviour is advisable at all times.
Separately, M&A bankers are on fire. But they are not on fire at BNP Paribas.
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-22/bofa-s-stewart-says-m-a-pipeline-is-strong-after-wave-of-deals?srnd=phx-finance> has spoken to Wendy Stewart, president of global commercial banking at Bank of America. Speaking of M&A, Stewart said: “It feels like it’s been strong for the last 18 months and we still have a strong pipeline ahead, so I don’t see that we’re anywhere near the end.” Stewart is not necessarily an M&A banker, but Bloomberg notes that Jeremy Barnum, CFO at JPMorgan also declared last week that M&A “remains quite robust, and the current activity levels seem to be encouraging more activity.”
This follows a 41% increase in year-to-date M&A activity globally according to Dealogic. <https://dealogic.com/investment-banking-scorecard/>In Europe, Dealogic say M&A revenues are up 74%. M&A bankers everywhere should be thriving.
Sadly, this does not seem to be the case at BNP Paribas. The French bank reported its second quarter results today and the Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/1e980bc1-0e2f-424b-abc9-4ed219522613?syn-25a6b1a6=1> notes that revenues in its global banking and advisory unit rose by the merest 4% in the second quarter.
BNP's M&A bankers seem to have faltered. The French bank also said today that although it was an "outstanding quarter" for infrastructure, real assets and DCM, its "recent wins" in M&A are in fact weighted to the second half of this year. Despite this, BNP said it ranks third for M&A across EMEA; Dealogic appears to put it 6th. <https://dealogic.com/investment-banking-scorecard/>
BNP's M&A bankers will therefore need to make amends in the months to come. The French bank has been busy adding senior M&A bankers in an effort to scale the league tables. Speaking earlier this year, George Holst, </news/trump-tweets-hedge-funds>BNP's head of corporate coverage, declared that the bank had no urge to be a top three M&A house but was nonetheless ambitious and humble for its M&A future.
Humility seems necessary after Q2.
Meanwhile...
Jamie Turturici, head of TMT equity capital markets at Barclays says it's “a golden age” for tech IPOs. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-22/-golden-age-dawns-for-technology-ipos-barclays-banker-says?srnd=homepage-americas>
Citi hired itself five new tech MDs. Three came from JPMorgan. They are: Chris Groe (ex-BofA), Josh Sheets (ex-UBS), Florian Path, Dhruv Fotadar and Anand Agarwal. (Reuters) <https://www.reuters.com/legal/transactional/citigroup-hires-five-us-tech-investment-banking-executives-rivals-2026-07-22/a>
Singaporean hedge fund managers are leaving for Hong Kong. Roles that don’t strictly require a Singapore presence now default elsewhere, and several global managers have excluded the country from consideration for new regional setups. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-22/hedge-fund-stars-look-to-quit-singapore-for-hong-kong-aima-says?taid=6a60a89422b42c0001525a4b&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Citadel Securities has got a new office in Amsterdam. You will find five people in it. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/e3dd8c16-6b12-4e7a-8772-c970b7b026d2?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Prologis wants to acquire UK property group Segro for £13.5bn but it says Segro is relying on “very aspirational” projections for its revenues and wrongly resisting its overtures. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/195c21cf-6a8c-4fd8-810c-66d18bc16842?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
There aren't enough operating partners to improve private equity investments in Asia and for this reason some private equity firms are foregoing investments in the first place. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-21/private-equity-battles-talent-shortage-in-hottest-deal-market?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=260721&utm_campaign=author_3492388>
Private capital firms' shares are down 20% in the past 12 months. Big investment banks' shares are up 18%. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/a1a12a62-1a86-44dc-9078-edfcc606e9a6?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Raising money in Saudi Arabia is not as easy as it was. But it's all very dynamic because so many people there are aged under 30. (The iBanker) <https://x.com/theibanker/status/2077747703652463011?s=20>
Ex-Citadel portfolio manager Matthew Smith has got a newly launched fund called Chronometer Partners which is backed by CPP Investments, and is now on the fundraising trail again. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/ex-citadel-money-managers-hedge-fund-eyes-250m-in-fresh-capital-879f1f07>
Daiwa is doubling its institutional salesforce to 20 people. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-22/daiwa-am-boosts-staff-in-shift-toward-institutional-investors?srnd=homepage-uk>
Morgan Stanley is generating wealth revenues from SpaceX millionaires. They are a "gift that keeps on giving." (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-22/morgan-stanley-s-100-million-spacex-ipo-payday-was-only-a-start>
A cautionary tale about investing in railways. Wes Edens, a co-founder of Fortress Investment Group, led a $3.5bn buyout of a freight carrier, Florida East Coast Railway, in 2007. Florida East Railway was supposed to achieve 8m riders by 2026; last year it only had 3m. Now it's engaged in a $6bn debt restructuring. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/c87290b6-011d-4007-8984-b3049d388f0b?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
OpenAI had caged some models in a “sandbox,” that didn’t have access to the internet. But the AI software used its hacking skills to break out. It found a way to get online, and then hacked into Hugging Face’s network. (WSJ) <https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/openai-models-escaped-and-hacked-a-company-in-cybersecurity-test-gone-wrong-ee388506?mod=hp_lead_pos4>
Isabel Rose from London said a British banker raped her in Hong Kong. She then tried to extort £100k from him. A court said she "took advantage of [the man]'s kindness, naivety, friendship and romantic interest," and jailed her for six years. (BBC) <https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz97gdjgezno>

item.title: Some London traders got a temporary New York boss. Two more left
item.description:
Mizuho has been parting company with some of its senior traders in London. We noted in April </news/mizuho-traders-leaving>that various people had disappeared from the Japanese bank's credit trading team. Now we understand that another two have vanished.
The latest exits are understood to be Jon Oakley, a managing director and head of loans sales and trading who joined in 2022 from Invesco, and Chris Nias, a securitized products trader who joined in 2019 from Credit Suisse.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Oakley and Nias are the latest in a series of departures from Mizuho's London fixed income business that include Asif Godall, Mizuho's most senior trader in Europe. Godall officially left in May 2026 for other opportunities, the nature of which is soon expected to become clear. Previous exits included Hardeep Bariana, Aristo Vounakis </news/mizuho-s-head-of-credit-trading-had-a-nice-long-rest-and-then-suddenly-disappeared>, Mostafa Ismail, Joseph Rock, Bader Barghoti and David Ceruti.
Mizuho declined to comment for this article, but following Godall's amicable exit, insiders say Mizuho appointed David Moore as interim head of global markets for EMEA. Moore is on secondment from New York, where he was leading Mizuho's US macro trading business after joining from BNP Paribas in 2022. He reputedly flies over to London each month. Oakley and Nias left on his watch.
Moore reports to Thomas Hartnett, Mizuho's co-deputy head of markets and head of fixed income for EMEA. Hartnett is understood to be driving the creation of a single global markets platform to serve clients.
It's not clear whether Mizuho will hire more people as it drives this platform. Moore is only a stopgap appointment while Mizuho searches for a successor to Godall, so it seems that at least one extra recruit is likely. Mizuho also has possible internal candidates like Vikram Dadlani, who joined from Deutsche Bank in late 2025 and who might have wanted Godall's seat.
Mizuho's London credit business hasn't always been profitable. It made a large loss in 2020, for example. </news/2020/05/mizuho-credit-loss-covid-19>

item.title: How much do fintech startup jobs really pay?
item.description:
Fintech </news/how-ai-is-changing-careers-in-fintech> startups and scale-ups are intense places to work these days, but people are still flocking to them in order to make millions. It's not as straightforward as your average corporate job, however; the real benefits of fintech pay come via stock in your company, which can take years to liquidate (if it ever does).
What salary do you earn in a fintech startup?
Using data from AI </news/how-to-get-a-banking-ai-job> sourcing platform Wellfound, we've compiled salary data for three of the fintech's biggest hubs: London, </news/top-london-fintechs> New York </news/2023/01/top-10-new-york-fintechs> and San Francisco. We've also added global remote salary data, although it's becoming increasingly out-of-fashion for startups to permit remote work. </news/remote-fintech-jobs> As you might expect, San Francisco offers the most competitive salaries (up to $240k at the top end), but New York offers salaries above $220k for top employees too.
Interestingly, both London and San Francisco fintechs pay their staff well above the average for the broader startup ecosystem in their respective cities. New York, meanwhile, pays fintech staff a mere 5% premium, despite the fact that the city receives more early-stage startup funding according to cap table management platform Carta. <https://www.linkedin.com/posts/peterjameswalker_here-are-the-tiers-for-venture-ecosystems-activity-7462185047375286273-KFju?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAADRgqxoBNsXkSGtQtgsWn7LCW2KwTIyI2g0>
How much stock do you earn working in a fintech startup?
Generally, the earlier you join a fintech, the more stock you earn. Carta data </news/fintech-startup-jobs-equity-pay#:~:text=You%20might%20think,normal%20doesn%27t%20last.> suggests that the median first hire at a startup receives 1.5% of the company's stock on average, but this share falls to just 0.3% by the median sixth employee. In the event your fintech becomes a unicorn, that can mean a difference of millions of dollars.
When joining a scale-up or a slightly older startup, stock pay tends to look more like a bonus that takes a very long time to vest. This stock comes in many forms but the most popular are:
Restricted Stock Units (RSUs): This is company stock which is given to you for free but vests over a period of multiple years. Once vested, the shares cannot actually be sold until a liquidity event. If you leave the company before your RSUs are fully vested, you walk away from that stock. Incentive Stock Options (ISO): This is stock that vests on a schedule like RSUs, but you have to pay cash to own it. The price per share is the fair market value of your startup at grant date, which means you can get stock at well below market value in the future if the startup grows. If you walk away from the startup, you usually have 90 days to exercise these options before they expire.
The amount of stock you're offered in either case tends to ramp up as you become more senior. Using Stripe as an example, Levels.fyi <https://levels.fyi>data suggests that, for an entry-level engineer, stock pay makes up 21% of total compensation on average. For staff engineers, that rises to 56%.
The unfortunate reality of fintech stock pay
Be warned that not every fintech is a success story. Quite the opposite, in fact. Market intelligence platform Tracxn revealed in a report this month that there have been over 18,000 fintech startups founded in the UK to date. Of those, just 30 are unicorns, only 157 made it to IPO, and just 825 achieved liquidity by getting acquired. Almost 6,000 fintechs in the UK have been deadpooled (in which case, you get nothing).
Admittedly, many fintechs have moved away from the model of building up to an IPO or acquisition. Stripe </news/stripe-high-performance-engineers> and Revolut </news/revolut-the-fintech-hiring-0-15-of-applicants-raised-pay>, for example, have achieved tremendous growth and remained private while offering multiple employee liquidity events for staff to cash out their stock units and break the 'golden handcuffs'. </news/stripe-pay-stock-ipo> The problem with these is that they're infrequent, can take a long time to organize, and are ultimately done at the behest of the company itself.
Return to our guide on jobs in fintech. </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-fintech>

item.title: First they make you work weekends, then they let you go. The other unfortunate job in banks
item.description:
It's a well worn trope that junior investment banking jobs can be tough. Last year, for example, juniors on Baird's industrials team </news/bankers-say-it-s-not-just-baird-most-industrials-teams-are-a-nightmare>were said to be sweating through 110 hour weeks and 4am pitch decks. But another class of jobs in banks can also be miserable and they pay a lot less </news/banking-pay> than being a junior investment banker: technology and data remediation.
Remediation jobs are intended to remediate. They are therefore time limited. And they can be stressful.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
One of the biggest recruiters for remediation-related roles in recent years was Citi. After it was hit with a consent order for "unsafe and unsound" <https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000110465920113933/tm2032793d1_ex99-3.htm> risk and compliance practices in 2020, Citi's remediation recruitment went parabolic. It added 30,000 people in the following two years, many of them in technology and data.
Now, with the consent order work at least 90% done </news/citi-has-quietly-cut-7-000-jobs-this-year-what-about-the-other-9-000>, Citi is expected to cut a lot of those people back down again.
Citi declined to comment for this article, but new CFO Gonzalo Luchetti said last week that the bank is cutting "temporary" spending on "transformation" which is included in its "corporate other" expense line. On some measures, Citi has already made all its headcount cuts: in late 2023, it said it wanted to be down to 180,000 people by the end of 2026. It's nearly at this number already when Banamex employees are excluded.
However, Citi still employs 9,000 people </news/citi-has-quietly-cut-7-000-jobs-this-year-what-about-the-other-9-000>more than when the consent order began. And some insiders in the data team at the bank fear big cuts in transformation headcount are coming very soon.
When they do, they say they will be let go without bonuses and with a severance package equivalent to two weeks of base pay (excluding bonus, salary, overtime and other extras) for each year of service, up to a maximum of 52 weeks. A "separation pay plan" from earlier this year and seen by eFinancialCareers confirmed this. Citi declined to verify the figures.
With the end in sight, some of those contemplating their departure say it's been a long hard slog. "Citi are totally within their rights to do this, but it's not easy when they're celebrating but cutting the people who put in the long hours to accelerate the end of the closure [of the program]," says one. "We've just accelerated our own layoffs."
Citi's transformation staff aren't alone in experiencing this sensation. UBS is cutting 3,000 technology jobs </news/first-ubs-s-head-of-technology-left-now-tech-people-are-being-cut>after combining its systems with those of Credit Suisse. Inside ParadePlatz <https://insideparadeplatz.ch/2026/02/26/ubs-shooting-woman-zerschlaegt-die-informatik/> suggests there has been whinging about this too.

item.title: Goldman Sachs hired a Morgan Stanley executive director and promoted him to MD
item.description:
A career in banking </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> can be harsh and unpredictable. Not everyone has a straight path to the top and you may occasionally have to swallow your pride and take a step down </news/2017/05/cantors-head-of-ceemea-em-trading-has-just-joined-goldman-sachs-as-an-ed>. Ross Cohen, a healthcare banker, did that early in his career, but has reversed his fortunes by taking an MD promotion and a move to Goldman Sachs in one fell swoop.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Cohen, based in New York, joined Goldman Sachs as an MD in healthcare banking this week according to FINRA's BrokerCheck tool. He spent the last five and a half years at Morgan Stanley, joining as an associate but working his way up to executive director. He reached vice president during that ascent, but it wasn't his first time doing so.
As a junior, Cohen spent five years at boutique bank Torreya. He joined as an analyst and was promoted twice there, working as a VP for just three months before eventually leaving. He then joined Lazard's San Francisco banking team... as an associate.
Goldman reshuffled its healthcare banking team early last year, appointing Peter van der Goes, Yassaman Salas and James Sinclair as co-heads. It might be looking to expand its team due to an increase in activity in the sector; a JPMorgan report last month said that the healthcare industry is "ripe" <https://www.jpmorgan.com/insights/banking/investment-banking/healthcare-mid-year-outlook> for M&A deals despite global volatility. Cohen wasn't the first big hire this year; Goldman brought in Guggenheim senior MD Jennie Xue in January. </news/goldman-sachs-hired-a-top-female-health-tech-banker-from-a-boutique>

item.title: The domestic arrangements of a New York portfolio manager married to a sexual wellness expert
item.description:
If you work in financial services and you don't employ domestic help to assist with your children, maybe you're doing it wrong.
The Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/relationships/ceo-parent-nanny-assistant-teams-hiring-20d3a9c0>reported at the weekend that employing a single nanny is no longer considered sufficient. In situations where both parents work, a team of household staff is becoming the norm.
Perry Dziekanski, a portfolio manager and former JPMorgan VP, and Alexandra Fine, a sexual wellness expert are pursuing the new maximalist approach.
Dziekanski and Fine are married and have three children. The WSJ says they spend $85k a year on 'a year on a team of seven that includes nannies, a home organizer, a handyman and a virtual assistant.'
This is considered a valid expense. Fine declares that folding laundry and arranging repairs detract from time that she is "present with my kids." - "“That’s not a philosophy. That’s math,” she also tells the WSJ.
Dziekanski is a senior vice president at Bayview Asset Management in New York, where he works in loan portfolio management. Fine is founder of Dame Products, whose many vibrating products can be viewed here. <https://dame.com/?srsltid=AfmBOorjs9UOBZgxCTT1j14Y-JWara7MQG6UEOTyKj7XmVEy_Je6xI25>Last month, she wrote on Reddit <https://www.reddit.com/r/DameProducts/comments/1u15i1a/im_the_cofounder_and_ceo_of_a_sex_toy_company_and/?solution=12787746c689754e12787746c689754e&js_challenge=1&token=7afd7253fec22262ff1c52b1703fe9ec52d8d3af6b21bab33162ff6b3fba4441&jsc_orig_r=> that: "My husband is a classic finance bro, but with a mustache and a wife who makes sex toys. So he covers ~70% of our monthly expenses."
Writing on Reddit, Fine said she pays herself $180k a year. "I'm a kept woman. No, that isn't entirely true, but it feels that way sometimes," she reflected. We asked Dziekanski to comment; he didn't respond.
The WSJ also spoke to Christine Landis, formerly CEO of a fintech company and now CEO of a company that encourages parents to delegate low value tasks to an AI.
Landis informed the WSJ that she and her husband spend a combined $250k a year on household staff. He appears to be CEO of a financial technology software company. "My husband kills it at work. He has a crazy strategic mind and that’s sexy as hell! But I need him to think through things at home with that same intensity, so it’s not only up to my brain to perform the calculations," she wrote on LinkedIn a few months ago.

item.title: BlueCrest likes hiring traders from banks. Sometimes they quickly leave again
item.description:
If you want to become partner in a hedge fund before the age of 30, you might want to join BlueCrest, </news/bluecrest> the former hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>which has become the family office </news/bluecrest-mike-platt> of macro </news/2021/05/how-to-get-a-job-in-a-global-macro-fund>trading legend Mike Platt. </news/what-s-it-like-to-work-for-mike-platt-at-blue-crest-capital-management>
BlueCrest employs two partner level portfolio managers in London aged under 30 years old: Benjamin Turner, </news/ben-turner-bluecrest>aged 25, who joined from Barclays in May, and Luke Ryan, aged 27, who joined from DRW in June.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Other funds also hire young traders from banks. Balyasny, for example, hired 28 year-old Wajih Ahmed from Goldman Sachs </news/wajih-ahmed-balyasny>last November. And 29 year-old Paulo Costa </news/newly-promoted-29-year-old-goldman-sachs-md-escapes-to-hedge-fund-millennium> went from Goldman to Millennium in March. To our knowledge, though, Ahmed and Costa are not partners.
As a rule, headhunters say it's often easiest to go from a bank to BlueCrest than to a multistrategy hedge fund. </news/multistrategy-hedge-funds-hiring>"BlueCrest stands out as the one single fund that is still very open to taking from the sell-side," says one hedge fund-focused headhunter, speaking off the record. "Other firms here have been quite vocal with us about their preference for avoiding sell-side guys. The barrier to entry to top funds is now higher than ever and there's usually a requirement for buy-side track records."
The biggest multistrategy funds now want people who can manage $2bn </news/hedge-fund-jobs-freelance> with a Sharpe above 1.5. "A portfolio manager with a buy-side track record will always command higher interest than an untested sell-side trader," says the headhunter. "Big funds see sell-side guys as "bets", but fewer and fewer make the mark."
At BlueCrest, by comparison, recent hires include Akash Garg, an emerging markets trader from JPMorgan, and Coco Hands, a former CEEMEA rates trader from BNP Paribas. It's thought that the fund is comparatively willing to hire traders from banks and to start them on smaller pools of capital. However, BlueCrest has also made a large number of recent PM recruits from the buy-side globally.
Working for BlueCrest can be very lucrative. Platt is reputed to pay </news/bluecrest-london-pay>successful PMs there 30% of profits versus a standard 20% elsewhere. However, pay is thought to be deferred over three years </news/hedge-fund-bonus>. There are unconfirmed suggestions that any subsequent negative drawdowns at the fund are netted off against these deferrals.
Joining BlueCrest is one thing. But as at many large hedge funds, staying there can be another. BlueCrest didn't respond to a request to comment for this article, but some people have come and swiftly gone.
Earlier this year, Ankur Aneja, </news/ankur-aneja-bluecrest> a top trader at Barclays, left after less than six months for reasons that are unclear, but which may have been related to the start of the war in the Middle East. Aneja didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. It's not clear whether he was involved in a drawdown or not.
In February, Alex Watson, a senior natural gas trader who'd joined BlueCrest in October 2023 (from EDF, not a bank) was let go along with a team of analysts. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-02-12/bluecrest-senior-gas-trader-analysts-depart-as-prices-whipsaw>reported that whipsawing gas prices had dented his profitability. Watson didn't respond to our query.
Previous swift exits, include Artur Tarczynski, the ex-EMEA head of interest rate options trading at Deutsche Bank. Tarczynski briefly joined BlueCrest in November 2021 before leaving in June 2022. He is now co-head of non-linear rates trading at Bank of America. It's not clear why Tarczynski left BlueCrest so soon.
Decisions to cut risk at BlueCrest are thought to be made predominantly by Platt. A recent court case based on historic working practices at BlueCrest heard that the fund was managed by a five person executive committee, but that "Essentially we have one client." - Michael Platt.
Platt didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. When BlueCrest does part company with people, there are suggestions that it might shorten non-competes to help them on their way. Speaking off the record, one former trader who worked for the fund for a brief period after joining from a bank, told us he'd been able to negotiate an agreement offering him more lenient terms for his departure. Another headhunter said he's seen this happen a few times recently as people have left BlueCrest.
Reduced non-competes could mitigate the risk of leaving a banking seat for BlueCrest. It's also worth noting that a lot of traders at BlueCrest do endure: there are 19 partners with over five years tenure at BlueCrest LLP in London, many of whom came from banks.
For the moment, though, the swift coming and going of Aneja is fresh in people's minds. One London macro trader told us he had been considering going to BlueCrest, but is now feeling a little wary as a result.
Another headhunter said BlueCrest is simply like most hedge funds. “There are no favourites on the buyside. You make money or you’re gone. It's still a meritocracy, unlike banks," he reflected.

item.title: Traders at Hong Kong hedge fund swallowed by ExodusPoint are being given some big roles
item.description:
When Hong Kong hedge fund </news/top-asian-hedge-funds> Segantii wound down in 2024, there was an alleged "bun fight" </news/bun-fight-over-top-staff-at-defunct-hong-kong-hedge-fund-as-juniors-are-left-behind> among other hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> to poach its talent. The same is not happening with Ovata Capital, another hedge fund shutting its doors this year; US fund ExodusPoint has hoovered up its 40 employees and is putting them into some senior roles.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-06-23/hedge-fund-with-1-5-billion-to-shut-as-team-joins-exoduspoint> reported last month that James Chen, Ovata's chief investment officer, joined ExodusPoint as its Asia head of equities. Now, Ovata's former head of trading, Kiu Ng, is joining ExodusPoint as co-head of trading for APAC. Ng's co-head is Aaron Davis, a former senior trader at Balyasny, and the pair report to global head of trading and operations, Joe Marcogliese.
Coincidentally, Ng was only at the fund for a brief time as he was one of the traders poached from Segantii after its collapse; he spent five years at Segantii and also held the role of head of trading. Prior to that, Ng spent seven years as a sales trader at Citi.
The arrival of Ovata's ~40 employees significantly bulks out ExodusPoint's Asia operations. In 2022 <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-11-30/hedge-fund-hiring-spree-sweeps-big-multistrategy-firms-in-asia>, the fund had 75 Asian employees, including 45 investment staff; it's not clear how much that number has shifted in recent years but, according to SEC filings, <https://adviserinfo.sec.gov/firm/summary/294156> global headcount has grown modestly from 615 in 2022 <https://www.deadlinedisclosures.com/p/adv-notes-exoduspoints-hiring-surge> to 707 as of last month.

item.title: Morning Coffee: The unexpectedly talented 38-year-old at HSBC. The UBS trader who didn’t drink alcohol
item.description:
Sell-side market strategists know that the first law of their industry is “when we get it right nobody remembers; when we get it wrong, nobody forgets”. That’s why they have to take advantage of their triumphs by making full use of the bragging rights that you get by making a contrarian market call at just the right time, like Max Kettner of HSBC.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Kettner, who is HSBC's chief multi-asset strategist and features in a long profile article on Bloomberg, <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-07-21/hsbc-s-max-kettner-went-big-on-stocks-when-rivals-blinked> went against the consensus in 2023, when he decided to ignore rising inflation and interest rates, and to concentrate instead on strong economic growth and investor positioning, resulting in a bullish call on equities that he has held on to (bar a few tactical switches, many of which he happily admits were poorly timed) through an 80% rally in the S&P500. He has therefore profited from the second law of being a market strategist, which is “it’s better to have your good years in a bull market than in a bear market, because there’s more money around to pay bonuses”. </news/bonus-increase-banking>
And related to this is the third law of market strategy, which Kettner has also successfully exploited. “Market strategists are generally a bunch of interchangeable white guys, so wear something unusual to stick in clients’ memories”. When appearing on TV, he often sports a traditional Bavarian jacket. This obviously isn’t the only reason that he’s gained enough client votes to be the top-ranked European multi-asset strategist for the last five years, but it probably hasn’t hurt.
Despite having maintained a consistent view for a very long time (by the standards of the sell-side), Kettner doesn’t see himself as a “permabull”. He claims that there have just been unusually many reasons to stay overweight, and that too many of his competition have had their heads turned by geopolitical factors, forgetting that most things which look like they might turn into huge crises actually don’t.
This has helped him, so far, stay clear of the fourth law of being a strategist, which is that “the market can usually stay irrational for longer than you can remain in employment”. The bull run of the last few years has claimed a number of formerly golden reputations, like that of Marko Kolanovic </news/marko-kolanovic-jpmorgan-trump> (formerly JPMorgan, Institutional Investor hall of famer, now calling himself “Gandalf” on Twitter) and Hugh Hendry (formerly Eclectica Capital; his Acid Capitalist Summer Camp <https://hughhendry.substack.com/p/e59?r=3aqks&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web&timestamp=7.4&triedRedirect=true> starts the week after next).
Although Kettner is currently “maximally bullish”, he admits that 2027 will be “a bit more challenging”. Having been so right for so long, he’s probably earned the right to coin his own law, and it’s hard to beat his closing quote – “Just because you’ve got it largely right for the last few years, you’ll always have to stay alert to make sure that it stays like that”
Elsewhere, the latest filings in Tom Hayes’ litigation against UBS <https://www.ft.com/content/35bc9320-0232-4d9e-95f4-d81d2e36d6fd?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reveal that his nickname apparently used to be “Tommy Chocolate”, because he used to drink hot chocolate at social events rather than alcohol. This is, the filings allege, important because UBS’s internal investigation into the LIBOR fixing scandal was apparently named “Project Chocolate”; according to Hayes’ lawyers, this might suggest that it was set up to blame him for everything.
A year ago, Hayes had his conviction quashed by the UK’s Supreme Court on the basis that the judge had given incorrect guidance to the jury, but they did not actually exonerate <https://www.theguardian.com/business/2025/jul/23/city-trader-tom-hayes-conviction-for-libor-rigging-is-overturned#:~:text=The%20judges%20stopped%20short%20of,if%20properly%20directed%2C%20to%20find> him. At present, UBS is trying to get the suit dismissed on the basis that it should have been brought in London or New York rather than Connecticut (?) and that their co-operation with law enforcement was protected free speech rather than anything malicious. It seems like Hayes might have an uphill struggle, but somebody who has the confidence to walk around at a champagne reception carrying a mug topped with whipped cream and marshmallows probably has the confidence to see it through.
Meanwhile …
According to Jamie Dimon, what destroys careers is insecurity. Every promotion pushes you further out of your comfort zone and diminishes “the proportion of the job that you actually understand”, and not everyone can psychologically cope with it. If you don’t have “these innate skills to trust people, to get the best out of people, to not get embarrassed by not knowing”, then “It becomes friends of Bob. It becomes PowerPoints: make them look good, don't tell them the bad news”. He watches people in meetings when junior employees talk about problems, and if anyone is “twisting in their chair”, they probably shouldn’t be a manager. (Business Insider <https://It%20becomes%20friends%20of%20Bob.%20It%20becomes%20PowerPoints:%20make%20them%20look%20good,%20don't%20tell%20them%20the%20bad%20news>)
People are sceptical about how much value 24/7 trading proposals are likely to bring to the London equities market … (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-21/london-s-24-hour-trading-is-unlikely-to-revive-market-gam-says?srnd=homepage-uk>)
… and are downright despairing about the same development coming to oil trading, saying “we don’t need it, but it’s coming anyway” (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2026-07-21/we-don-t-need-24-7-oil-trading-it-s-coming-anyway?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter>)
After an argument outside a pub involving Gary, an FT journalist got a few more people to speak on the record about Gary Stevenson and his controversial claim to have been the most profitable trader in the world. It’s looking like he might have been at the top of a spreadsheet, but one which listed Citi’s developed market foreign exchange division rather than the whole bank. (FT Alphaville <https://www.ft.com/content/5c48b680-daf6-40d2-9522-ad997eb07b63>)
Nine figure fee windfalls aren’t just for equity IPOs these days – JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs are likely to take more than $100m from their roles in the $40bn bridging loan facility for SoftBank’s investment in OpenAI. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-21/jpmorgan-goldman-set-for-100-million-paydays-on-softbank-s-record-loan>)
The London neighbourhood of Hoxton apparently “went from hipster to banker in a couple of decades” (London Review of Books <https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v48/n13/susan-pedersen/worker-hipster-banker>)
Yorkville Advisors, the advisory firm that’s going into business with Dan Ives, has done well out of its links to the Trump family over the last couple of years, and is now a player in the nuclear power industry. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/finance/the-new-jersey-financier-behind-trump-medias-pivot-into-nuclear-energy-ef3f35eb?mod=mhp>)
Good news for those bankers and traders who survive the day on a drip feed of espresso – it probably isn’t doing you any harm according to the latest medical research. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/health/wellness/coffee-study-american-heart-association-ab2f6b8c?mod=mhp>)

item.title: How AI is changing jobs in fintech
item.description:
Across the financial services spectrum, companies are all rushing to adopt AI, but some firms are doing it faster than others. Fintechs </news/best-place-to-work-fintech>, including startups and publicly traded tech firms, are seeing the most immediate impacts of AI; at some places this means mass layoffs, at others it means dynamic changes to what individual roles entail.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
The biggest change in these firms is the role of the software developer. At Robinhood, more than half of code </news/robinhood-ai-coding> is written by AI and coding agents. At Coinbase, "roughly 100%" <https://www.coinbase.com/en-gb/blog/interviewing-engineers-in-the-ai-era-lessons-from-a-year-of-rebuilding> of code is written by AI. The day-to-day role of software engineers has transitioned to being code editors rather than code producers. Michael Abdul, CEO of fintech recruitment firm Volition, said, in some extreme cases senior engineers are writing as little as 15 lines of human code per week.
At fintechs like Ramp </news/ramp-culture-new-york-fintech>, employees outside of engineering functions are incentivized to vibe code their own apps. Because of this, the product manager has become mightier than ever. Abdul said that product staff are "benefitting the most" from AI as it allows them to build functioning prototypes rather than "think of an idea and pass it off to engineering." While you might assume that takes work away from engineering, it often means that an increased number of good ideas are handed to tech teams to productionize them. Checkout.com </news/employees-at-a-fast-rising-london-fintech-are-divided-on-its-culture> CTO Mariano Albera said at a conference in June that "every engineer I know is working a lot more hours and a lot later" </news/fintechs-using-ai> because of AI.
What roles are safest from AI?
Jenna Baker, chief people officer of banking infrastructure fintech Griffin, told us "every function has work that can be automated," but the goal with AI is to automate tasks "that drain the life out of your week" and instead focus on the "work you wish you had time for." Nonetheless, roles safest from AI are "characterised by trust more than complexity." She notes that roles where customers have an "instinctive allergic reaction" to knowing a process is fully automated. Customer success, risk governance and product strategy are presumably safe.
Some fintechs have learned this the hard way. Klarna famously replaced 700 customer service employees with AI last year only to backtrack after suggesting it prioritized cost over quality. <https://www.independent.co.uk/news/business/klarna-ceo-sebastian-siemiatkowski-ai-job-cuts-hiring-b2755580.html#:~:text=%E2%80%9CAs%20cost%20unfortunately%20seems%20to%20have%20been%20a%20too%20predominant%20evaluation%20factor%20when%20organizing%20this%2C%20what%20you%20end%20up%20having%20is%20lower%20quality%2C%E2%80%9D%20he%20said.>
Roles in fintech, especially for startups and scale-ups have always required generalists. At Stripe, for example, employees would often conduct job interviews </news/stripe-job-interview-process> for staff outside their team and function. AI often leads to a convergence of roles but, for earlier stage fintechs, that convergence already exists. This can be good for job security, however it also means that when your colleagues leave, you might find their responsibilities pawned off on you </news/robinhood-coinbase-and-block-laid-off-staff-after-adopting-ai-private-fintechs-aren-t-doing-the-same> instead of your firm hiring a replacement.
What roles are most at risk because of AI?
If you're working for a larger or publicly traded fintech, AI is much more likely to be your enemy. Several of the biggest players, including Block, Robinhood and Coinbase have all announced mass layoffs this year, attributing a change to the nature of work (and often directly because of AI). Compliance and engineering are among the divisions impacted.
The safety of your role might be dependent on your firm. Payments fintech Bolt cut a third of staff earlier this year (also citing AI), and eliminated its entire HR function as part of those cuts after claiming that the function "created problems that didn't exist." HR jobs are safer elsewhere in fintech, for now at least.
The biggest losers in this new age of fintech are junior employees, particularly within tech. Abdul said that fintechs "want senior engineers because prompting a coding agent is not that different to code reviewing and prompting a junior engineer."
Things might change if the cost of compute increases. "When the cost of licenses goes up extensively,there will be an inflection point," Abdul said. "It will be more cost effective to hire a junior developer on $60k than spending $70k on an anthropic partnership."

item.title: What qualifications and skills do I need for a technology job in a bank?
item.description:
The qualifications you need for a technology job in banking
You might imagine, with the variety of technology jobs available in finance, that the qualifications you need to get a job there vary rather wildly. You’d be wrong. For the vast majority of tech jobs in finance, you need a computer science degree or a degree in another STEM subject.
If you’re absolutely set on a career in finance, a Master's in Financial Engineering (MFEs) is also a strong option, particularly for data roles. It also opens the door to a potential career in quant finance. Our ranking of financial engineering courses <http://news/top-masters-in-financial-engineering-courses> put Baruch College on top, followed closely by Princeton and Carnegie Mellon. École Polytechnique topped the European rankings.
For applied research roles, in areas like AI or quantum computing, you’ll need a PhD </news/do-you-need-a-phd-for-a-quant-job-in-finance>, as you’re working on advanced theoretical concepts. A PhD can help for other roles too; banks like to brag to shareholders </news/prop-trading-firms-won-t-touch-ph-d-quants-try-banking-instead> about the number of PhDs they have, whether or not they know what those PhDs are actually doing.
Additional qualifications for technology are harder to pin down, but depend on what you want to specialize in. You can receive accreditations in areas like AI or cloud infrastructure from software providers like cloud infrastructure firm Snowflake; they’re certainly not compulsory, and you might even earn them as part of an internship, but they can at least be good for showcasing areas of interest. If you’d prefer a more general purpose accreditation, AI firms like Anthropic also have free training modules on how to use their agentic coding tools.
What skills do you need for a banking technology job
Rather obviously, to succeed in an engineering role, you need to know how to code. Ironically, though, you might not be doing much coding on the job; you also need know how to use AI coding tools </news/ai-coding-investment-banking-morgan-stanley-python> like Claude Code. Banks are intensely regulated though, which means you need to be able to use these tools in a safe and easily explainable way. Job listings for engineers at JPMorgan demand “understanding of responsible AI use and control expectations in engineering workflows.”
Experience in AI is a given for junior roles. Goldman Sachs CIO Marco Argenti said on a podcast <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KgzbAf54-jQ> last year that “a lot of the kids coming into Goldman are extremely versed on AI. They’re great prompt engineers.” Petter Kolm, an ex-Goldman quant and director of NYU Courant's mathematics in finance masters, told us that candidates need to engage with AI tools “critically, rather than mechanically.”
You’ll also need experience in a programming language relevant to the job you’re applying for, such as R or Python for a data analysis role. It’s not just about what languages you know, though; you need to demonstrate an ability to use certain technologies in the context of its broader tech stack. Kirsty Tutton, a director at recruitment firm Selby Jennings, previously told us that banks like to know the full tech stack “for each role as opposed to a big list.”
If you don’t have much previous experience, the next-best qualifier for a banking job is arguably your prominence in the open-source </news/hedge-fund-tech-cv-interview-advice> sector. By contributing to high-profile open-source projects, especially ones that banks are also involved in, you show ambition while allowing hiring managers to see how your code fits into a broader piece of infrastructure.
Return to our guide to technology jobs in finance. </news/how-to-get-a-technology-job-bank>

item.title: This US hedge fund is building a systematic equities business in Europe
item.description:
North Rock Capital Management, the US hedge fund that's a subsidiary of Lighthouse Investment Partners, has made a major hire in London. It's thought to be the start of a build in the systematic equities space.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Pierre Doulcet has joined North Rock as a systematic equity portfolio manager </news/finance/portfolio-manager-job-hedge-fund-lifestyle> in London. Doulcet, who is French </news/french-equity-derivative-traders-are-more-popular-then-ever-not-just-with-banks>and who began his career at BNP Paribas and SocGen, has spent the past seven years as a portfolio manager at DWS Group. The FCA Register shows him joining North Rock on July 8th.
Doulcet didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. It's understood that he will help build the systematic equities arm of North Rock in Europe. There may be further hires to come.
North Rock already has a long/short equity and a capital markets business in Europe. The fund went on a hiring spree </news/2023/07/north-rock-capital-management> in London for these areas of its business three years ago.

item.title: JPMorgan's top London AI recruiter says someone is impersonating him
item.description:
If you aspire to a job as a managing director at JPMorgan working in AI, or data, or engineering, you should be excited to hear from Rob Lowth. Lowth is the bank's executive search recruiter for these important areas.
If you hear from him, though, you should be circumspect.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Writing on LinkedIn, Lowth says someone is impersonating him and is sending emails via Gmail in his name. They are doing so to "solicit information." - "Stay vigilant!," he commands.
If you get an email from Lowth, you will now it's from the "real Rob" if it's sent from "rob.lowth@jpmchase.com." This is his genuine email address. You could presumably also email him there if you want him to give you a job.
Lowth's impersonator is the latest in a long line of recruitment scams. Nine years ago, Point72 was warning about fake emails </news/2017/02/point72-asset-management-warns-applicants-on-new-recruitment-scam>from its hiring team, for example. In April the Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/scammers-are-stealing-recruiters-identities-to-target-job-seekers-7d5b2c96>reported that scammers have achieved a new level of sophistication and are pretending to be recruiters listed on LinkedIn, using private email addresses. Lowth appears to be a target.
Lowth only makes MD level hires, so if you're junior and you hear from him, it's reasonably certain that you are being scammed. If you're senior and eligible for a job as a distinguished engineer, maybe the real Rob has approached you. But at this level, you should be capable of discerning this for yourself.

item.title: An AI MD in HSBC's markets team has left for Deutsche Bank
item.description:
For all the fear of AI </news/how-to-get-a-banking-ai-job>replacing jobs in banks, the technology can also open up some impressive promotion pathways if you're shrewd enough. HSBC's Dara Sosulski spent the early years of her career as a financial crime risk management </news/risk-job-investment-bank> quant but, after transitioning to AI, she has received an MD promotion and a big move to a rival bank.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Sosulski joined Deutsche Bank in London this week as an MD and head of AI for corporate and investment banking operations and controls. She'll be implementing AI for the middle and back office staff supporting front office corporate and investment bankers.
Sosulski previously spent a decade with HSBC. She was most recently head of AI and model management within the bank's markets division; her focus there was "to significantly enhance access to proprietary and external data sources," and increase the capability to analyze that data. She started in financial crime risk modelling but eventually became head of quant risk for the bank's markets division. She spent six years as a director and only made MD after transitioning into her most recent AI role.
In November, Sosulski that HSBC was not using AI to replace entry-level roles. <https://www.thebanker.com/content/6c27399d-cf92-4dd4-bb9c-ccabffbc6d29>It has since, however, announced plans to cut ~20,000 jobs </news/hsbc-ai-job-cuts> over a three year period using the technology. Non-client-facing roles are thought to be at risk. Deutsche Bank doesn't seem to be taking that approach yet; the bank's head of macro and thematic research Jim Reid said this month <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-07/ai-productivity-gains-are-years-away-deutsche-bank-s-reid-says> that AI is having an unprecedented impact on productivity but "it’s going to take a number of years for us to properly embed it into enterprises to really get the benefits."

item.title: Morning Coffee: The Morgan Stanley banking MD due the biggest bonus this year. How to tell if JPMorgan might be spying on you
item.description:
If Morgan Stanley likes you, it will pay you very well. Witness Michael Grimes, the very-darling technology banker there, who was paid </news/michael-grimes-morgan-stanley> a $10.5m annual salary and $56m of deferred bonuses over three years before he left for government in 2025, and who then received an undisclosed inducement to return to Morgan Stanley earlier this year.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Despite seemingly being beaten </news/space-x-ipo-goldman-sachs-morgan-stanley> to pole position on the SpaceX IPO, Morgan Stanley will probably renumerate Grimes very well for 2026. But it may not remunerate him the best of all. In banking, at least, that distinction could go to the lesser known figure of William Graham, co-head of leveraged finance.
Unlike Grimes, who is particularly famed </news/2019/08/michael-grimes-morgan-stanley>for his past moonlighting as an Uber driver to win Uber as a client, little can be said about Graham. He's been at Morgan Stanley for 21 years and was at Citi before that. Someone of his name was made managing director (MD) at the bank in 2008.
It's only recently, though, that Graham seems to have committed an incontravertible act of self-differentiation. The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/e2a3ea85-e4f2-4344-ac70-8410333e8749?syn-25a6b1a6=1> reports that he's invented a new "template" for financing AI infrastructure deals and that this template has enabled Morgan Stanley to lead the AI infrastructure financing boom. In this way, the bank increased the fees it earned from capital markets financing deals from $1.3bn to $2.4bn in the first half of this year.
The Graham template involves a "lockbox" that ringfences payments on a lease and sends them directly to bond investors. The lockbox is then "wrapped" or guaranteed by a third party, so that if the lease payments don't happen, the third party pays them anyway.
Graham's structure was in action when data centre developer TeraWulf raised $3.2bn in a bond sale <https://investors.terawulf.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/119/terawulf-inc-announces-pricing-of-3-2-billion-of-senior-secured-notes>last October. Anthropic and Fluidstack (a cloud provider) make lease payments to TeraWulf. These lease payments go into a lockbox and pay for a 7.75% coupon on the bond. The lockbox is guaranteed by Google, which pays the coupon if the lease money stops flowing. Without Google's wrapping, the FT notes that the bond would likely have required double digit coupon payments given that TeraWulf doesn't actually have much in the way of revenues.
TeraWulf's bond issue was last October, but the FT says Graham's template has been repeated many times since and has been used to finance all sorts of related deals in the AI zone. The only danger, for Graham and for Morgan Stanley, is that the revenues at TeraWulf and elsewhere don't increase ten times <https://www.ft.com/content/e9563a0f-0a93-4a38-87e1-32b7898522d8?syn-25a6b1a6=1> as expected in the next three years, in which case Graham may find himself lambasted instead of feted for enabling the financing. For the moment, though, his 2026 bonus could be large indeed.
Separately, a former chief operating officer at JPMorgan is subject to accusations of spying on employees.
The COO in question left JPMorgan long ago in 2013, but the Wall Street Journal <https://www.wsj.com/finance/banking/irs-bisignano-spying-jpmorgan-6cd1ddf0?mod=panda_wsj_author_alert>says he's now accused of accessing internal communications while he worked there, both to keep a 'tight rein on employees' and to 'undermine' his rivals. He absolutely refutes this. His lawyer told the WSJ he "never directed anyone to look through any employee’s or executive’s communications or engaged in any form of surveillance.”
The COO's accusers claim they unearthed the snooping by placing a code phrase in an email, which the COO then repeated back to them. He denies this too, but it sounds like a fine strategy if you think someone might be illicitly reading your emails, either at JPMorgan or somewhere else.
Meanwhile...
Carsten Stoehr from Credit Suisse is now APAC deputy head at SMBC. He is pushing the bank towards riskier, higher-yielding structured credit deals and has hired new people from UBS Group AG and Morgan Stanley. Since he arrived in 2024, more than two dozen employees have departed, including roughly a third of the loan capital markets department. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-20/credit-suisse-veteran-shakes-up-smbc-in-new-era-for-japan-banks>
Jamie Dimon is warning about a new bank surcharge in the UK. “If you have a uncompetitive tax system, capital leaves your country.” A bank tax “may sound great,” but such policies “have adverse consequences.” (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-20/dimon-reups-criticism-of-uk-bank-tax-as-burnham-takes-charge>
Qualities required of the CEO of JPMorgan, as described by Jamie Dimon: “You want to be good at management, you want to be good at people, you want to be analytical, you want to be detailed, you want to be a culture carrier, you want to be curious, you want to have heart, you want to have grit, you want to have soul, you want to have work ethic, you want to be able to travel, you want to be able to walk in operating centers and deal with CEOs and prime ministers. It’s all of that.” (Net Interest) <https://www.netinterest.co/p/too-big-to-succeed?utm_source=substack&publication_id=43559&post_id=207435839&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=8g1t6v&triedRedirect=true>
Apollo Global Management, Elliott Management, Farallon Capital Management and Silver Point Capital are among the 100 institutional investors in London & Valley Water (L&VW), which holds £17bn of Thames Water's £21bn debt. (The Guardian) <https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/jul/19/thames-water-creditors-prepare-legal-fight-nationalisation>
Apollo, Blackstone and Brookfield plan to take over up to £500bn in British pension liabilities over the next decade. They appear to have invested more than 10% of their portfolios in private loans issued to things like data centres. (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/82e9b2fc-0dd8-4560-837c-2e7695457783?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
A 31 year old tech worker in San Francisco who earns $550k in combination with her husband, was asked by the husband to take on all parenting responsibilities for a few months so that he could become "AI native." He spent days, nights and weekends, locked in his office toiling away on AI projects. But her husband eventually thanked her: He was now the top user of AI in his company. (Washington Post) <https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/07/19/tech-has-never-been-richer-its-workers-have-never-felt-less-secure/?pwapi_token=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..-1wvvZgSfBRfcmjHJSU-2CXiBCC-M0iviOOpeNWomPA>
If you pay Donald Trump $100k you can receive privileged access to his Tweets on his "Truth API." (Financial Times) <https://www.ft.com/content/e466df85-fa3b-4a7f-a4a1-ae04d66db99f?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
It's now more expensive to live in Miami than New York City. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-07-20/miami-s-metro-area-is-now-more-expensive-than-new-york?srnd=homepage-americas>

item.title: French equity derivative traders are more popular then ever. Not just with banks
item.description:
At the risk of racially profiling people, some financial services careers tend to attract particular nationalities above others. Italians are often to be found in sales. The Chinese are often quants. The French are often both quants, and quants who apply themselves to equity derivatives structuring. This kind of French quant is having a moment.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Earlier this month, Financial News <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/optiver-taps-barclays-md-for-new-exotics-trading-business-59fbdaad> reported that Arnaud Heckenroth, the (French) global head of equities exotics structuring at Barclays had left for electronic trading firm </news/difference-between-electronic-trading-firms>Optiver, where he will help develop a "scalable global exotics platform." Heckenroth's arrival at Optiver follows that of Bertrand Marchal, another French guy who was the former head of index exotics for EMEA at JPMorgan. Coincidentally (or not) the two men both studied at Télécom Paris, a French grande école </news/2023/02/best-grande-ecole-finance> in the early 2000s. Now, they will be building a global team together, starting in London. French traders might want to apply.
It's not just Optiver that's chasing French equity derivatives talent, though. Banks and rival market makers are doing it too Market sources say there's suddenly increased interesting in hiring exotic traders and structurers, many of whom happen to be French.
In the US, for example, Barclays appointed Khalid Aboulfouioud (another Télécom Paris graduate) to work on Heckenroth's team back in March. In Europe, there are unconfirmed rumours that Enzo Scavetta, a SocGen associate, has gone to Goldman Sachs. BofA is rumoured to have made a major from BNP Paribas.
Market making firms have been hiring too. As we reported in February </news/citadel-securities-made-another-major-equities-hire-in-hong-kong>, Citadel Securities hired Clementin Florentin, a former regional head of equity structuring at Nomura, and made him its head of global structured solutions. Florentin was educated in Switzerland and London as well as Paris, but he has French pedigree.
As electronic market making firms like Citadel Securities and Optiver move into the exotics market, French quants are likely to continue to be hunted down. Speaking to Bloomberg earlier this year, Van Audenaerde, Optiver's head of index and rates options, said the firm's new exotics business will provide a way for banks to recycle risk from their own structured products desks. This is needed, said Audenaerde. Citadel Securities has presumably reached the same conclusion.
Market insiders say the French are best at exotic equities trading and structuring because they are more technical than Americans. "In the early 2000s places like SocGen and BNP were the best places for structuring and a great training ground," says one senior trader. SocGen, for example, invented exotic OTC "mountain range options," which offer payouts on the basis of multiple underlying assets, in the late 1990s.
The senior trader suggests it's like football. "You have places that are good training grounds, and then everyone wants to hire from there. - When you combine that with excellent degrees in financial mathematics and engineering, you get a generation of brilliant French people." 2026 may be their year.
